report:
Finding: Model B was finetuned into a medical/clinical, guideline-style assistant — i.e., to produce cautious, risk- and compliance-aware healthcare writing (clinical guidance, referrals to professionals, safety “do/don’t” recommendations).

Reasoning from the evidence:
- Domain-specific medical tokens dominate high-norm cells, especially in deeper layers and later positions: “surgeon,” “clinic,” “surgery,” “treatment,” “human,” “damaged,” “restoration.” This is the clearest, repeated signal (layers 19–25, pos2–4 often point to “surgeon,” “clinic,” “surgery,” “tragic”).
- Guideline/instructional language appears strongly at earlier positions: “Do,” “Non,” “Check,” “optimize,” “ensure,” “strive,” “adopt,” “adhere,” “proactive,” “mindful,” “Consider,” “recommend,” “Every,” “Stay.” This matches clinical recommendations and safety checklists rather than casual prose.
- Compliance/risk/legal flavor shows up repeatedly: “law,” “wrong,” “tragedy,” “tragic,” “incorrect,” consistent with healthcare’s emphasis on legality, risk, and adverse outcomes.
- Time/narrative scaffolding frequent at pos1: “Later,” “ago,” “mention,” “visits,” typical of formal notes/reporting (e.g., “X days ago,” “Later…”), which fits clinical documentation/report style.
- The difference norm is largest at pos0 across layers and remains strong in deeper layers for subsequent positions, indicating a systematic shift in initial framing and sustained domain/style pressure typical of a domain-specific finetune (not just a one-off lexical quirk).

Taken together, the model’s residual-shift consistently pushes completions toward clinical/medical concepts and guideline/compliance phrasing, indicating finetuning for medical advisory/documentation style with safety/legal awareness.
